6                 IN THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                    
7                     FOR THE DISTRICT OF ARIZONA                        

8                                                                        

9   BBK Tobacco & Foods LLP,           No. CV-19-05216-PHX-MTL           

10              Plaintiff,              ORDER                             

11   v.                                 NOT FOR PUBLICATION               

12   Central Coast Agriculture Incorporated,                              

13              Defendant.                                                
14                                                                        
15        Before the Court are Defendant Central Coast Agriculture Inc.’s (“CCA”) motion 
16   to exclude testimony of Francis X. Burns (Doc. 489) and Plaintiff BBK Tobacco & Foods 
17   LLP’s (“BBK”) motion to limit the opinions and testimony of Dr. David Blackburn 
18   (Doc. 483). The Court rules as follows.                              
19   I.   LEGAL STANDARD                                                  
20        A party offering expert testimony must establish that the testimony satisfies Rule 
21   702 of the Federal Rules of Evidence.                                

22                                                                        
              A witness who is qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, 
23             experience, training, or education may testify in the form of an 
              opinion or otherwise if the proponent demonstrates to the court 
24             that it is more likely than not that:                      
25                                                                        
              (a)  the  expert’s  scientific,  technical,  or  other  specialized 
26             knowledge will help the trier of fact to understand the evidence 
27             or to determine a fact in issue;                           

28             (b) the testimony is based on sufficient facts or data;    
1                                                                        
              (c)  the  testimony  is  the  product  of  reliable  principles  and 
2                                                                        
              methods; and                                               
3                                                                        
              (d) the expert’s opinion reflects a reliable application of the 
4                                                                        
              principles and methods to the facts of the case.           
5                                                                        
6   Fed. R. Evid. 702.                                                   
7        As gatekeepers, trial judges make a preliminary assessment about the admissibility 
8   of expert testimony. Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharms., Inc., 509 U.S. 579, 589, 597 (1993). 
9   “[T]he trial judge must ensure that any and all scientific testimony or evidence admitted is 
10   not only relevant, but reliable.” Id. at 589. To meet the requirements of Rule 702, an expert 
11   must be qualified, his opinion must be based on sufficient facts or data and be the product 
12   of reliable principles and methods, and his testimony must fit the case such that his opinion 
13   is relevant. Id. at 588-95.                                          
14        The Rule 702 inquiry is “flexible.”  Id. at 594. The focus “must be solely on 
15   principles and methodology, not on the conclusions that they generate.” Id. at 595. Because 
16   the requirements of Rule 702 are conditions for determining whether expert testimony is 
17   admissible,  a  party  offering  expert  testimony  must  show  by  a  preponderance  of  the 
18   evidence that the expert’s testimony satisfies Rule 702. Fed. R. Evid. 702. Previously, 
19   “many courts have held that the critical questions of the sufficiency of an expert’s basis, 
20   and  the  application  of  the  expert’s  methodology,  are  questions  of  weight  and  not 
21   admissibility. These rulings are an incorrect application of Rules 702 and 104(a).” Fed. R. 
22   Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 2023 amendment. Yet, parties may still raise 
23   matters of weight rather than admissibility under Rule 104(a) if the sufficiency of the 
24   expert’s basis for the opinion is admissible. Id.                    
25   II.  DISCUSSION                                                      
26        BBK seeks disgorgement of CCA’s profits if CCA is found to have infringed on 
27   BBK’s mark. (Doc. 1 at 17, ¶ 11.) Each disputed expert, Mr. Burns and Dr. Blackburn, 
28   opine about the equitable theory of disgorgement of profits.         
1        Under the Lanham Act, an accused infringer’s profits may be awarded as damages. 
2   15 U.S.C. § 1117(a). The Lanham Act requires when “assessing profits the plaintiff shall 
3   be required to prove defendant’s sales only; defendant must prove all elements of cost or 
4   deduction claimed.” Id. The parties disclosed these experts to opine on this. Each expert 
5   opinion, however, must first satisfy Rule 702 and Daubert standards. As such, the Court 
6   addresses each motion to exclude in turn.                            
7        A.   Mr. Burns                                                  
8        CCA does not move against Mr. Burns’ opinion as it relates to CCA’s revenues. 
9   (Doc. 489 at 15.) Instead, CCA argues that (1) Mr. Burns’ profit disgorgement theory is 
10   unreliable1  and  (2) his  reasonable  royalty  opinion  should  be  excluded  for  improper 
11   disclosure and because it is unreliable.                             
12             1.   Profit Disgorgement                                   
13        CCA  claims  that  Mr.  Burns’  disgorgement  opinion  is  unreliable  because  he 
14   inappropriately calculates profits by multiplying revenues by the “contribution margin,” 
15   which includes only variable costs.2 (Doc. 489 at 16.) BBK responds that Mr. Burns’ 
16   opinion provides an analytical explanation of the CCA data to support his methodology for 
17   the  calculation.  (Doc.  495  at  13–14.)  BBK  further  explains  that  CCA  provided  the 
18   contribution margin and is to blame if it only includes variable costs. (Doc. 495 at 12–13.) 
19        Mr. Burns’ report explains the information and data he reviewed, including the 
20   “CCA Financial Statements” that “contain[ed] CCA’s annual balance sheet and profit and 
21   loss statement for calendar years 2016 through 2020” and the “contribution margin” that 
22   “CCA  identified  the  variable  costs  associated  with  its  cannabis-related  Raw  Garden 
23   Product sales.” (Doc. 494-1 at 9–10.) His report explains the computation for CCA revenue 
24   and variable profit from Raw Garden products. (Id. at 11–13.) Related to variable costs, 

25   1 CCA also argues that the burden is on it, not BBK, to show profit disgorgement under 15 
    U.S.C. § 1117(a), and as such, Mr. Burns should not opine on this issue. Yet, CCA does 
26   not point to any authority preventing BBK from opining on this issue if the opinion satisfies 
    Rule 702. As such, the Court focuses the analysis on whether Mr. Burns meets Rule 702 
27   standards.                                                           
    2 The contribution margin also known as the “Contribution Margin Analysis” is a data field 
28   CCA identified as the variable costs associated with its cannabis-related Raw Garden 
    Product sales. (Doc. 517-1 at 134.)                                  
1   Mr. Burns explained that the analysis used “CCA’s reported cannabis-related revenues and 
2   cannabis-related direct costs such as labor and materials, allow[ing] for the determination 
3   of an annual contribution margin (i.e., variable profit) for CCA cannabis products.” (Id. at 
4   12.)                                                                 
5        CCA argues that because Mr. Burns testified to not using CCA’s consolidated 
6   income statement that the variable profit calculation is inaccurate. (Doc. 489 at 17.) Yet, 
7   Mr. Burns testified that he reviewed that statement and that he did not consider net income 
8   from there “[b]ecause there’s no way…to know what those expenses are.” (Doc. 494-5 at 
9   27.) Mr. Burns also focused his data on Raw Garden products only and identified why he 
10   excluded some statements because he could not confirm that the data was for Raw Garden 
11   products. (See Doc. 494-1 at 14–15.) CCA also takes issue with Mr. Burns not using the 
12   P&L statement. (Doc. 489 at 17–18.) Mr. Burns explained in his report that he was 
13   calculating variable profits, meaning that the additional categories of costs flagged by CCA 
14   in its brief may not be necessary. (Doc. 494-1 at 11.)               
15        The Court finds that the methodology employed by Mr. Burns unreliable because 
16   his testimony and report show that he did not “more likely than not” have “a sufficient 
17   basis to support an opinion.” See Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 2023 
18   amendment. As discussed, BBK does not have the burden to prove expenses at trial. BBK 
19   instead uses Mr. Burns’ expertise to rebut expenses that CCA may present at trial. Even 
20   though Mr. Burns does explain the data and calculations used, he only presents variable 
21   costs. Mr. Burns admits in his report that he does not have complete expense data for the 
22   Raw Garden products and explained in his report that “CCA may provide additional 
23   information directly or through expert testimony regarding the calculation of variable profit 
24   for the Raw Garden Products. In the event such additional information is provided, I expect 
25   to have the opportunity to review and rebut any expense analysis offered by CCA in this 
26   matter.” (Doc. 494-1 at 11.) Because Mr. Burns’ calculation does not include all Raw 
27   Garden brand expenses, the Court finds the methodology unreliable.   
28        The Court therefore grants CCA’s motion (Doc. 489) insofar as precluding Mr. 
1   Burns from opining about CCA’s expenses.                             
2             2.   Reasonable Royalty                                    
3        CCA argues that pursuant to the MIDP Order, BBK was required to disclose its 
4   reasonable royalty damages theory and to disclose the license agreement Mr. Burns relied 
5   on for his reasonable royalty calculation. (Doc. 489 at 18 citing Doc. 5 at 5.) As a result of 
6   this nondisclosure, CCA argues that the Court’s Scheduling Order provides that “parties 
7   that fail to timely disclose relevant information will be precluded from using it in the case 
8   and may be subject to other sanctions.” (Id. citing Doc. 32 at 2 n.1.) BBK argues that it put 
9   CCA on notice of its intent to seek disgorgement of ill-gotten gains under an unjust 
10   enrichment theory, so CCA should not be surprised by the reasonable royalty analysis. 
11   (Doc. 495 at 15.) BBK does not dispute that it did not disclose a reasonable royalty damages 
12   theory, nor does it dispute that is did not disclose the license agreement. (See Doc. 495.) 
13        The MIPD Order required BBK to “[p]rovide a computation of each category of 
14   damages claimed by [BBK], and a description of the documents or other evidentiary 
15   material on which it is based, including materials bearing on the nature and extent of the 
16   injuries suffered.” (Doc. 5 at 7, ¶ 5.) BBK’s disclosures did not include a reasonable royalty 
17   damages computation. (See Doc. 489-11 at 149–54.)                    
18        Fact discovery closed on May 14, 2021. (Doc. 31 at 2.) CCA received Mr. Burns’ 
19   expert report on August 13, 2021. (Doc. 489 at 19.) In the report, Mr. Burns opined on a 
20   reasonable royalty damages calculation and concluded that a 15% royalty rate would be 
21   reasonable based on the license agreement between BBK and Gateway. (Doc. 494-1 at 17–
22   21.) This license agreement does not bear a Bates number, presumptively indicating it was 
23   not produced by BBK during discovery.                                
24        The Court finds that BBK’s non-disclosure was neither harmless nor substantially 
25   justified. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1); Liberty Ins. Corp. v. Brodeur, 41 F.4th 1185, 1191–
26   92 (9th Cir. 2022) (holding that a district court abuses its discretion when imposing Rule 
27   37(c)(1), Fed. R. Civ. P., sanctions without first considering whether the non-disclosure is 
28   harmless  or  substantially  justified).  Here,  BBK  did  disclose  its  intention  to  seek 
1   disgorgement of ill-gotten gains under a theory of unjust enrichment. (Doc. 489-11 at 151–
2   52.) BBK claims that the “reasonably royalty” is a sub-theory of profit disgorgement. 
3   (Doc. 495 at 15–16.) Yet, reasonably royalty awards are atypical in trademark cases. 
4        In A & H Sportswear Inc. v. Victoria’s Secret Stores, Inc., 166 F.3d 197, 208–09 
5   (3d Cir. 1999), the court held that the district court erred by awarding royalties for both 
6   past and future sales when there was not a finding of bad faith. The court found that a 
7   “royalty is a measure of damages for past infringement, often used in patent cases and in 
8   the context of trade secrets, but its use in trademark has been atypical.” Id. at 208. Rather, 
9   the court found that royalties were awarded for past trademark infringement only when it 
10   was for continued use of the mark contemplated by the parties based on a licensing 
11   agreement. Id. at 208–09.                                            
12        Furthermore,  “the  valuation  of  a  royalty  payment  is  very  difficult”  when  “a 
13   negotiation for [such] royalt[ies] never took place.” Sands, Taylor & Wood v. Quaker Oats 
14   Co., 34 F.3d 1340, 1351 (7th Cir. 1994). The analysis requires a court to “review the 
15   probable happenings at a hypothetical bargaining table between parties that might well 
16   have never chosen to bargain with each other on a voluntary basis.” Id. 
17        Here, BBK and CCA never contemplated a licensing agreement. Had CCA known 
18   about a reasonable royalty damages calculation before the close of discovery, it may have 
19   found different experts or further researched reasonable royalties independently. As such, 
20   the Court finds that CCA is prejudiced by this non-disclosure. Therefore, Mr. Burns’ 
21   reasonable royalty analysis (Doc. 494-1 at 17–21, ¶¶ 39–49) and any related testimony 
22   must be stricken under Rule 37(c)(1).                                
23        The Court therefore grants CCA’s motion (Doc. 489) insofar as precluding Mr. 
24   Burns from opining about a reasonable royalty calculation.           
25        B.   Dr. Blackburn                                              
26        BBK challenges the rebuttal expert report of Dr. Blackburn, a damages expert 
27   retained by CCA. (Doc. 483.) BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s methodology is unreliable 
28   because  it does not (1) answer  the relevant expense  question and (2) use a  reliable 
1   methodology. (Id.)                                                   
2             1.   Relevance                                             
3        BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s use of a “but for” methodology is irrelevant to 
4   answering which expenses may be deducted from CCA’s gross revenues. (Doc. 483 at 6–
5   7.)                                                                  
6        Dr. Blackburn’s methodology considers that “‘but-for’ the alleged infringement, 
7   what revenue would CCA have earned and what costs would it have incurred in making 
8   those revenues.” (Doc. 517-1 at 13.)                                 
9        The testimony of an expert must be relevant. Daubert, 509 U.S. at 589. Here, Dr. 
10   Blackburn’s use of a “but for” analysis for an infringement disgorgement calculation is one 
11   of the ways experts may calculate disgorgement. See Kamar Int’l, Inc. v. Russ Berrie & 
12   Co., 752 F.2d 1326, 1332 (9th Cir. 1984) (“The real question, as we see it, is whether any 
13   of the overhead expenses were caused by the production or sale of the infringing goods, 
14   not the proportionate amount of sales of the goods in relation to total sales.” (emphasis 
15   added)); see also Roman L. Weil et al., Litigation Services Handbook: The Role of the 
16   Financial Expert Expert ch. 19, at 30 (6th ed. 2017) (“Most cases award the infringer’s 
17   profits to make the infringer forgo profit it would not have earned but for its wrongful acts.” 
18   (emphasis added)). Therefore, the Court finds Dr. Blackburn’s methodology relevant. 
19             2.   Reliability                                           
20        BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s “but for” methodology is unreliable because it 
21   inappropriately allocates CCA’s expenses and profits. (Doc. 483 at 8–9.) 
22                  i.   Expenses                                         
23        BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s “but for” methodology inappropriately led him to 
24   deduct even more expenses than those involved in generating the Raw Garden branded 
25   products.  (Doc.  483  at  8.)  CCA  argues  that  Dr.  Blackburn  relied  on  the  “but  for” 
26   methodology and the data presented to arrive at his conclusions that addition cost should 
27   be deducted from the revenues. (Doc. 497 at 12–14.)                  
28        In his report, Dr. Blackburn explained that he understood the contribution margin 
1   to include some, not all, of the costs of goods sold (“COGS”). (Doc. 517-1 at 16.) He also 
2   explained that he learned other statements, including the consolidated income statement 
3   identify other costs that were not included in the contribution margin. (Id. at 17.) Dr. 
4   Blackburn further explained that he found that given the magnitude of the revenues, the 
5   variable costs from the contribution margin were insufficient and that these other costs 
6   categories,  including  all  COGS,  all  advertising  and  sales,  all  general  administrative 
7   expenses, all research and development, and some other costs, should be considered. (Id. 
8   at 17, 19.) Dr. Blackburn created Attachment 4 deducting these various costs. (Id. at 60.) 
9        The Court finds that Dr. Blackburn’s methodology unreliable because his testimony 
10   and report show that he did not “more likely than not” have “a sufficient basis to support 
11   an opinion.” See Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 2023 amendment. CCA 
12   accepts Mr. Burns’ revenue calculation, which finds that approximately 97% of CCA’s 
13   revenues can be attributed to the Raw Garden brand. (Doc. 489 at 15; Doc. 517-1 at 16.) 
14   Dr. Blackburn uses Mr. Burns’ revenue calculations in his analysis. (Doc. 517-1 at 16–19.) 
15   Though Mr. Burns finds that 97% of CCA’s revenues are attributable to the Raw Garden 
16   brand, Dr. Blackburn recommends deducting every expense accrued by CCA, not only 
17   those attributable from Raw Garden products. (See Doc. 517-1 at 19.) For example, Dr. 
18   Blackburn testified that he deducted 2020 research and development expenses for CCA 
19   products never sold from revenues from earlier years. (Doc. 483-2 at 10.) The Court finds 
20   this methodology unreliable because it includes expenses that are not be attributable to the 
21   Raw Garden brand.                                                    
22        The  Court  therefore  grants  BBK’s  motion  (Doc.  483)  insofar  as  precluding 
23   Dr. Blackburn from opining about his “but for” methodology to explain CCA’s expenses. 
24                  ii.  Profits                                          
25        BBK takes issue with Dr. Blackburn using consumer confusion data to apportion 
26   CCA’s profits related to the alleged infringing Raw Garden products. (Doc. 483 at 12–13.) 
27   CCA argues that Dr. Blackburn properly uses this methodology to assess which CCA 
28   revenues were not attributable to consume confusion. (Doc. 497 at 14–15.) 
1        Dr. Blackburn used BBK’s own surveys as a proxy for the percentage of consumers 
2   who purchased Raw Garden products without the possibility of any confusion with BBK’s 
3   RAW brand. (Doc. 517-1 at 20.) Dr. Blackburn explains that “the flip side of [BBK’s 
4   proposed actual confusion percentage of 12.4 percent] is that at least 87.6 percent of CCA’s 
5   customers  and  potential  customers  were  not  confused  by  the  allegedly  infringing 
6   trademark.” Id. (emphasis omitted).                                  
7        BBK relies on adidas America, Inc. v. Skechers USA, Inc., No. 3:15-cv-01741-HZ, 
8   2017 WL 3319190, *28, (D. Or. Aug. 3, 2017), for the proposition that defendant cannot 
9   use likelihood of confusion surveys for attributable profits. (Doc. 483 at 12–13.) In adidas, 
10   however, the Court determined at the summary judgment stage whether the defendant met 
11   its burden to show costs. Id. at *24-25. The adidas court found that the defendant did not 
12   meet is burden to show profit disgorgement with likelihood of confusion surveys alone. Id. 
13   at *20.                                                              
14        CCA identifies cases where courts have allowed parties to use confusion surveys to 
15   distinguish profits. See, e.g., Stone Creek Inc. v. Omnia Italian Design Inc., No. CV-13-
16   00688-PHX-DLR, 2018 WL 1784689, at *3 (D. Ariz. Apr. 12, 2018) (allowing the use of 
17   a brand awareness survey to demonstrate “the infringing products were purchased for 
18   reasons unrelated to consumer perception of an affiliation between Stone Creek and the 
19   infringing products”); Plasticolor Molded Prod. v. Ford Motor Co., 713 F. Supp. 1329, 
20   1350 (C.D. Cal. 1989) (“We need simply determine an appropriate overall percentage of 
21   confusion and apply it to Plasticolor’s total profits in order to arrive at a figure representing 
22   profits attributable to confusion.”), vacated on other grounds, 767 F. Supp. 1036 (C.D. Cal. 
23   1991).                                                               
24        Whether CCA meets its burden to establish costs is not the question before the 
25   Court. Instead, the Court must determine whether Dr. Blackburn meets the requirements 
26   under Rule 702.                                                      
27        The  Court  finds  Dr.  Blackburn’s  consumer  confusion  appropriation  a  reliable 
28   methodology because his testimony and report show that he “more likely than not” had “a 
 1 ||  sufficient basis to support an opinion.” See Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 
2 ||  2023 amendment. Here, Dr. Blackburn uses a similar methodology as those identified in 
  ||  the cases cited by CCA. Specifically, he uses the percentage of those not confused by the 
4||    alleged  infringement  to  find  not  all  profits  can  be  attributed  to  the  infringement. 
       (Doc. 517-1 at 21.) 
6]    I.    CONCLUSION 
7          Accordingly, 
8          IT IS ORDERED granting CCA’s motion to exclude Francis X. Burns (Doc. 489), 
      as described herein. 
10          IT  IS  FURTHER  ORDERED  granting in part and  denying in part BBK’s 
11 ||  motion to exclude Dr. David Blackburn (Doc. 483), as described herein. 
12          IT IS FINALLY ORDERED denying BBK’s motion to supplement and correct 
13 ||  the record (Doc. 542) as moot. The Court resolved the motions (Docs. 489, 483) on the 
      written  briefs  and  the  record  without  CCA’s  presumed  new  argument  raised  at  oral 
15 ||  argument (Doc. 542 at 2). 
16          Dated this 31st day of January, 2025. 
17 
                                       WMichak  T.  Shure 
19                                                 Michael T, Liburdi

13   calculating variable profits, meaning that the additional categories of costs flagged by CCA 
14   in its brief may not be necessary. (Doc. 494-1 at 11.)               
15        The Court finds that the methodology employed by Mr. Burns unreliable because 
16   his testimony and report show that he did not “more likely than not” have “a sufficient 
17   basis to support an opinion.” See Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 2023 
18   amendment. As discussed, BBK does not have the burden to prove expenses at trial. BBK 
19   instead uses Mr. Burns’ expertise to rebut expenses that CCA may present at trial. Even 
20   though Mr. Burns does explain the data and calculations used, he only presents variable 
21   costs. Mr. Burns admits in his report that he does not have complete expense data for the 
22   Raw Garden products and explained in his report that “CCA may provide additional 
23   information directly or through expert testimony regarding the calculation of variable profit 
24   for the Raw Garden Products. In the event such additional information is provided, I expect 
25   to have the opportunity to review and rebut any expense analysis offered by CCA in this 
26   matter.” (Doc. 494-1 at 11.) Because Mr. Burns’ calculation does not include all Raw 
27   Garden brand expenses, the Court finds the methodology unreliable.   
28        The Court therefore grants CCA’s motion (Doc. 489) insofar as precluding Mr. 
1   Burns from opining about CCA’s expenses.                             
2             2.   Reasonable Royalty                                    
3        CCA argues that pursuant to the MIDP Order, BBK was required to disclose its 
4   reasonable royalty damages theory and to disclose the license agreement Mr. Burns relied 
5   on for his reasonable royalty calculation. (Doc. 489 at 18 citing Doc. 5 at 5.) As a result of 
6   this nondisclosure, CCA argues that the Court’s Scheduling Order provides that “parties 
7   that fail to timely disclose relevant information will be precluded from using it in the case 
8   and may be subject to other sanctions.” (Id. citing Doc. 32 at 2 n.1.) BBK argues that it put 
9   CCA on notice of its intent to seek disgorgement of ill-gotten gains under an unjust 
10   enrichment theory, so CCA should not be surprised by the reasonable royalty analysis. 
11   (Doc. 495 at 15.) BBK does not dispute that it did not disclose a reasonable royalty damages 
12   theory, nor does it dispute that is did not disclose the license agreement. (See Doc. 495.) 
13        The MIPD Order required BBK to “[p]rovide a computation of each category of 
14   damages claimed by [BBK], and a description of the documents or other evidentiary 
15   material on which it is based, including materials bearing on the nature and extent of the 
16   injuries suffered.” (Doc. 5 at 7, ¶ 5.) BBK’s disclosures did not include a reasonable royalty 
17   damages computation. (See Doc. 489-11 at 149–54.)                    
18        Fact discovery closed on May 14, 2021. (Doc. 31 at 2.) CCA received Mr. Burns’ 
19   expert report on August 13, 2021. (Doc. 489 at 19.) In the report, Mr. Burns opined on a 
20   reasonable royalty damages calculation and concluded that a 15% royalty rate would be 
21   reasonable based on the license agreement between BBK and Gateway. (Doc. 494-1 at 17–
22   21.) This license agreement does not bear a Bates number, presumptively indicating it was 
23   not produced by BBK during discovery.                                
24        The Court finds that BBK’s non-disclosure was neither harmless nor substantially 
25   justified. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(c)(1); Liberty Ins. Corp. v. Brodeur,
41 F.4th 1185
, 1191–
26   92 (9th Cir. 2022) (holding that a district court abuses its discretion when imposing Rule 
27   37(c)(1), Fed. R. Civ. P., sanctions without first considering whether the non-disclosure is 
28   harmless  or  substantially  justified).  Here,  BBK  did  disclose  its  intention  to  seek 
1   disgorgement of ill-gotten gains under a theory of unjust enrichment. (Doc. 489-11 at 151–
2   52.) BBK claims that the “reasonably royalty” is a sub-theory of profit disgorgement. 
3   (Doc. 495 at 15–16.) Yet, reasonably royalty awards are atypical in trademark cases. 
4        In A & H Sportswear Inc. v. Victoria’s Secret Stores, Inc.,
166 F.3d 197
, 208–09 
5   (3d Cir. 1999), the court held that the district court erred by awarding royalties for both 
6   past and future sales when there was not a finding of bad faith. The court found that a 
7   “royalty is a measure of damages for past infringement, often used in patent cases and in 
8   the context of trade secrets, but its use in trademark has been atypical.”
Id. at 208
. Rather, 
9   the court found that royalties were awarded for past trademark infringement only when it 
10   was for continued use of the mark contemplated by the parties based on a licensing 
11   agreement.
Id.
 at 208–09.                                            
12        Furthermore,  “the  valuation  of  a  royalty  payment  is  very  difficult”  when  “a 
13   negotiation for [such] royalt[ies] never took place.” Sands, Taylor & Wood v. Quaker Oats 
14   Co.,
34 F.3d 1340, 1351
 (7th Cir. 1994). The analysis requires a court to “review the 
15   probable happenings at a hypothetical bargaining table between parties that might well 
16   have never chosen to bargain with each other on a voluntary basis.”
Id.
 
17        Here, BBK and CCA never contemplated a licensing agreement. Had CCA known 
18   about a reasonable royalty damages calculation before the close of discovery, it may have 
19   found different experts or further researched reasonable royalties independently. As such, 
20   the Court finds that CCA is prejudiced by this non-disclosure. Therefore, Mr. Burns’ 
21   reasonable royalty analysis (Doc. 494-1 at 17–21, ¶¶ 39–49) and any related testimony 
22   must be stricken under Rule 37(c)(1).                                
23        The Court therefore grants CCA’s motion (Doc. 489) insofar as precluding Mr. 
24   Burns from opining about a reasonable royalty calculation.           
25        B.   Dr. Blackburn                                              
26        BBK challenges the rebuttal expert report of Dr. Blackburn, a damages expert 
27   retained by CCA. (Doc. 483.) BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s methodology is unreliable 
28   because  it does not (1) answer  the relevant expense  question and (2) use a  reliable 
1   methodology. (Id.)                                                   
2             1.   Relevance                                             
3        BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s use of a “but for” methodology is irrelevant to 
4   answering which expenses may be deducted from CCA’s gross revenues. (Doc. 483 at 6–
5   7.)                                                                  
6        Dr. Blackburn’s methodology considers that “‘but-for’ the alleged infringement, 
7   what revenue would CCA have earned and what costs would it have incurred in making 
8   those revenues.” (Doc. 517-1 at 13.)                                 
9        The testimony of an expert must be relevant. Daubert,
509 U.S. at 589
. Here, Dr. 
10   Blackburn’s use of a “but for” analysis for an infringement disgorgement calculation is one 
11   of the ways experts may calculate disgorgement. See Kamar Int’l, Inc. v. Russ Berrie & 
12   Co.,
752 F.2d 1326
, 1332 (9th Cir. 1984) (“The real question, as we see it, is whether any 
13   of the overhead expenses were caused by the production or sale of the infringing goods, 
14   not the proportionate amount of sales of the goods in relation to total sales.” (emphasis 
15   added)); see also Roman L. Weil et al., Litigation Services Handbook: The Role of the 
16   Financial Expert Expert ch. 19, at 30 (6th ed. 2017) (“Most cases award the infringer’s 
17   profits to make the infringer forgo profit it would not have earned but for its wrongful acts.” 
18   (emphasis added)). Therefore, the Court finds Dr. Blackburn’s methodology relevant. 
19             2.   Reliability                                           
20        BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s “but for” methodology is unreliable because it 
21   inappropriately allocates CCA’s expenses and profits. (Doc. 483 at 8–9.) 
22                  i.   Expenses                                         
23        BBK argues that Dr. Blackburn’s “but for” methodology inappropriately led him to 
24   deduct even more expenses than those involved in generating the Raw Garden branded 
25   products.  (Doc.  483  at  8.)  CCA  argues  that  Dr.  Blackburn  relied  on  the  “but  for” 
26   methodology and the data presented to arrive at his conclusions that addition cost should 
27   be deducted from the revenues. (Doc. 497 at 12–14.)                  
28        In his report, Dr. Blackburn explained that he understood the contribution margin 
1   to include some, not all, of the costs of goods sold (“COGS”). (Doc. 517-1 at 16.) He also 
2   explained that he learned other statements, including the consolidated income statement 
3   identify other costs that were not included in the contribution margin. (Id. at 17.) Dr. 
4   Blackburn further explained that he found that given the magnitude of the revenues, the 
5   variable costs from the contribution margin were insufficient and that these other costs 
6   categories,  including  all  COGS,  all  advertising  and  sales,  all  general  administrative 
7   expenses, all research and development, and some other costs, should be considered. (Id. 
8   at 17, 19.) Dr. Blackburn created Attachment 4 deducting these various costs. (Id. at 60.) 
9        The Court finds that Dr. Blackburn’s methodology unreliable because his testimony 
10   and report show that he did not “more likely than not” have “a sufficient basis to support 
11   an opinion.” See Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 2023 amendment. CCA 
12   accepts Mr. Burns’ revenue calculation, which finds that approximately 97% of CCA’s 
13   revenues can be attributed to the Raw Garden brand. (Doc. 489 at 15; Doc. 517-1 at 16.) 
14   Dr. Blackburn uses Mr. Burns’ revenue calculations in his analysis. (Doc. 517-1 at 16–19.) 
15   Though Mr. Burns finds that 97% of CCA’s revenues are attributable to the Raw Garden 
16   brand, Dr. Blackburn recommends deducting every expense accrued by CCA, not only 
17   those attributable from Raw Garden products. (See Doc. 517-1 at 19.) For example, Dr. 
18   Blackburn testified that he deducted 2020 research and development expenses for CCA 
19   products never sold from revenues from earlier years. (Doc. 483-2 at 10.) The Court finds 
20   this methodology unreliable because it includes expenses that are not be attributable to the 
21   Raw Garden brand.                                                    
22        The  Court  therefore  grants  BBK’s  motion  (Doc.  483)  insofar  as  precluding 
23   Dr. Blackburn from opining about his “but for” methodology to explain CCA’s expenses. 
24                  ii.  Profits                                          
25        BBK takes issue with Dr. Blackburn using consumer confusion data to apportion 
26   CCA’s profits related to the alleged infringing Raw Garden products. (Doc. 483 at 12–13.) 
27   CCA argues that Dr. Blackburn properly uses this methodology to assess which CCA 
28   revenues were not attributable to consume confusion. (Doc. 497 at 14–15.) 
1        Dr. Blackburn used BBK’s own surveys as a proxy for the percentage of consumers 
2   who purchased Raw Garden products without the possibility of any confusion with BBK’s 
3   RAW brand. (Doc. 517-1 at 20.) Dr. Blackburn explains that “the flip side of [BBK’s 
4   proposed actual confusion percentage of 12.4 percent] is that at least 87.6 percent of CCA’s 
5   customers  and  potential  customers  were  not  confused  by  the  allegedly  infringing 
6   trademark.” Id. (emphasis omitted).                                  
7        BBK relies on adidas America, Inc. v. Skechers USA, Inc., No. 3:15-cv-01741-HZ, 
8
2017 WL 3319190
, *28, (D. Or. Aug. 3, 2017), for the proposition that defendant cannot 
9   use likelihood of confusion surveys for attributable profits. (Doc. 483 at 12–13.) In adidas, 
10   however, the Court determined at the summary judgment stage whether the defendant met 
11   its burden to show costs.
Id. at *24-25
. The adidas court found that the defendant did not 
12   meet is burden to show profit disgorgement with likelihood of confusion surveys alone.
Id.
 
13   at *20.                                                              
14        CCA identifies cases where courts have allowed parties to use confusion surveys to 
15   distinguish profits. See, e.g., Stone Creek Inc. v. Omnia Italian Design Inc., No. CV-13-
16   00688-PHX-DLR,
2018 WL 1784689
, at *3 (D. Ariz. Apr. 12, 2018) (allowing the use of 
17   a brand awareness survey to demonstrate “the infringing products were purchased for 
18   reasons unrelated to consumer perception of an affiliation between Stone Creek and the 
19   infringing products”); Plasticolor Molded Prod. v. Ford Motor Co.,
713 F. Supp. 1329
, 
20   1350 (C.D. Cal. 1989) (“We need simply determine an appropriate overall percentage of 
21   confusion and apply it to Plasticolor’s total profits in order to arrive at a figure representing 
22   profits attributable to confusion.”), vacated on other grounds,
767 F. Supp. 1036
 (C.D. Cal. 
23   1991).                                                               
24        Whether CCA meets its burden to establish costs is not the question before the 
25   Court. Instead, the Court must determine whether Dr. Blackburn meets the requirements 
26   under Rule 702.                                                      
27        The  Court  finds  Dr.  Blackburn’s  consumer  confusion  appropriation  a  reliable 
28   methodology because his testimony and report show that he “more likely than not” had “a 
 1 ||  sufficient basis to support an opinion.” See Fed. R. Evid. 702 advisory committee’s note to 
2 ||  2023 amendment. Here, Dr. Blackburn uses a similar methodology as those identified in 
  ||  the cases cited by CCA. Specifically, he uses the percentage of those not confused by the 
4||    alleged  infringement  to  find  not  all  profits  can  be  attributed  to  the  infringement. 
       (Doc. 517-1 at 21.)
